feet.label: Well-made leather sandals with fitted straps.

head.label: Hair kept short and oiled, in the Greco-Roman style of wealthy townsmen.

hold.label: A scroll or account record, standing for the wage books and contracts of an estate.

figures.name: A wealthy landowner

over.label: A heavy wool mantle (himation) dyed purple, an expensive dye. Tassels are included on the assumption that he is a Jewish man; the letter's audience and the rich addressees are debated.

figures.signals: Fine linen and dyed wool showed wealth and leisure. James 5:2 mentions moth-eaten clothing, so stored garments were a sign of riches.

under.label: A long inner tunic of fine linen, probably imported or finely woven, called a chiton in Greek.

figures.who: James 5:1-6 addresses rich people who hold back the wages of field workers and live in luxury.

feet.label: Often barefoot in the fields, though some labourers had simple sandals.

head.label: A simple cloth wrapped on the head against the sun.

hold.label: A basket for carrying cut grain, standing for reaping work.

figures.name: A day labourer who harvested the fields
figures.signals: Plain undyed cloth marked a poor working person. Day labourers were paid daily, and Jewish law (Deuteronomy 24:15) called for paying wages on the same day.

under.label: A knee-length tunic of coarse undyed wool or linen, belted at the waist for work.

figures.who: James 5:4 describes the workers whose unpaid wages 'cry out' against the rich.

head.label: A linen headcloth, a common covering for men in the eastern Mediterranean.

hold.label: A small jar of olive oil, used for anointing the sick as described in James 5:14.

figures.name: A village elder (presbyteros)

over.label: A wool mantle in a natural brown, with tassels on the assumption of a Jewish setting. Early Christian dress was not distinct from ordinary dress.

figures.signals: Nothing in his clothing set him apart from other townspeople. His role came from his standing in the community.

under.label: A long wool or linen tunic reaching the ankles, modest and plain.

figures.who: James 5:14 tells the sick to call the elders of the church, who pray and anoint with oil.

foods.name: Harvested grain
foods.text: Wheat and barley were reaped by hand, and the workers in James 5:4 are described as having reaped the fields.

foods.name: Olive oil
foods.text: Pressed from olives, it was used in cooking, lamps and medicine, and James 5:14 mentions anointing the sick with it.

foods.name: Barley and wheat bread
foods.text: Daily bread was baked from the grain that labourers harvested, so unpaid wages meant hunger.

foods.name: Meat from fattened animals
foods.text: James 5:5 speaks of fattening hearts 'in a day of slaughter', which draws on the image of animals fed for the butcher.

foods.name: Rain water
foods.text: James 5:7 refers to the early and late rains that farmers waited for, which filled cisterns and watered crops.

foods.name: Figs and early fruit
foods.text: Fruit was part of the 'precious fruit of the earth' that the farmer waits for in James 5:7.

objects.name: Wages and hoarded silver
objects.text: James 5:3 says gold and silver have 'rusted', a figure for wealth that was stored rather than used.

objects.name: Oil flask
objects.text: A small clay or stone container held the olive oil used for anointing in James 5:14.

objects.name: Sheep and fattened animals
objects.text: Livestock stood for the estates of the rich, and the 'day of slaughter' in James 5:5 uses this farm image.

objects.name: Plow and farm tools
objects.text: A wooden plow with an iron tip, pulled by oxen, prepared the fields that the farmer in James 5:7 waits on.

objects.name: Home of the sick person
objects.text: The elders in James 5:14 would probably visit a house of mudbrick or stone with a flat roof.

objects.name: Harvest basket
objects.text: Woven baskets carried cut grain and fruit, and they stand for the labourers' work in James 5:4.

context.text: In first-century Palestine, wealthy owners often held large farms worked by hired laborers and tenants. Day laborers lived hand to mouth and needed each day's pay to eat. Withheld wages could mean real hunger for a family.
context.title: Day laborers and large estates

context.text: The Torah required that a poor hired worker be paid on the same day, before sunset (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15). James 5 echoes this concern. Hearers familiar with Scripture would have recognized the standard being invoked.
context.title: Paying wages promptly

context.text: Farming in Israel depended on seasonal rain. The early rains came in autumn and softened the ground for sowing. The late rains came in spring and filled out the grain. A farmer's patience in waiting for them was a familiar image.
context.title: Early and late rains

context.text: Wealth was stored as grain, fine garments and precious metals. Garments could be eaten by moths, and metals could tarnish. James uses these everyday images of decay to describe hoarded riches.
context.title: Wealth in grain, cloth and metal

context.text: Early Jewish-Christian communities were led by elders. Oil was used in daily life as medicine and in religious practice. Christians have since read the passage on anointing the sick in different ways, and traditions still differ on its meaning.
context.title: Elders, prayer and anointing with oil

context.text: James points to the prophets and to Job as examples of endurance. Job's story was well known in Jewish tradition. Elijah, mentioned later in the chapter, appears in 1 Kings 17-18, where drought and rain are central.
context.title: Job and the prophets as examples

context.text: James uses the phrase 'Lord of Sabaoth,' a Greek form of a Hebrew title often translated 'Lord of Hosts.' It appears in the prophets and in Isaiah 5:9. It describes God as commander of heavenly armies.
context.title: Lord of Hosts

firstHearers.point: Oaths were part of everyday speech
firstHearers.text: People swore by heaven, earth or the temple to back up their word. James tells them not to swear, which echoes Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:33-37. Hearers would have heard it as a call to plain honesty.

firstHearers.point: Illness was often seen as tied to the community
firstHearers.text: Sickness could carry shame or suspicion of sin, and care was usually handled by family and neighbors. Calling the elders brought the whole community into the situation. It was a communal act, not a private one.

firstHearers.point: The Lord's coming was expected soon
firstHearers.text: Early Christians commonly expected the return of Jesus within their own lifetimes. This gave the call for patience a sense of urgency. It also gave the warnings to the rich a sharper edge.

firstHearers.point: The audience was probably Jewish-Christian and scattered
firstHearers.text: James opens by addressing 'the twelve tribes in the Dispersion.' Hearers lived across the Mediterranean world and knew the Hebrew Scriptures well. Allusions to the prophets, Job and Elijah would have been immediately recognizable.

scene.heading: A Field Hand's Wages, Unpaid
scene.text: You stand at the edge of a large estate in the hill country of Galilee or Judea, probably in late summer. The barley and wheat have been cut, and dry stubble crunches under your sandals. The air smells of dust, straw and sweat. Day laborers in rough wool tunics walk back toward the village, thin and tired. Their hands are cracked from the sickle. Beyond them stands the owner's house, built of whitewashed stone, with a storehouse beside it. Inside, grain is heaped in sacks and jars. Folded cloaks lie stacked in a chest, and a few look moth-chewed. Coins sit in a locked box. The workers have not been paid. Some wait by the gate. Others sit in the shade of a fig tree and share flat bread and olives. Far off, a farmer looks up at the sky. He is waiting for the autumn rains to soften the hard ground. Everyone is watching the horizon, and the dry wind blows steadily across the fields.

timeline.event: Elijah's ministry, with the drought in 1 Kings 17-18
Book of Job reaches its final written form
Jesus is crucified, traditionally dated to around this year
James, brother of Jesus, leads the Jerusalem church until his death, traditionally in 62 AD
The Letter of James is written; authorship and date are debated
timeline.when: Probably mid-1st century to early 2nd century (debated)

timeline.event: First Jewish Revolt against Rome; Jerusalem and its temple are destroyed

date.label: c. AD 40s–90s (uncertain)
date.note: The letter has no internal date, so the setting depends on who wrote it, and scholars disagree about that.

setting.period: The Roman Empire rules the eastern Mediterranean, and Jewish communities live under Roman provincial authority in Judea and scattered across the empire.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.role: James is traditionally associated with Jerusalem as the letter's place of origin. Chapter 5 does not name it, but the anointing and elder practices reflect a Jewish-Christian community setting.

places.modern: Jewish communities outside Judea, location unspecified
places.name: The Twelve Tribes in the Dispersion
places.role: The letter is addressed to Jewish believers scattered outside the homeland. Antioch in Syria is shown only as one plausible centre of such a community; the text does not say where the readers lived.

places.name: Mount Carmel region / Land of Israel (Elijah's setting)
places.role: Elijah is cited as an example of effective prayer. The drought and rain recalled here come from the Elijah stories in 1 Kings 17–18, which include Mount Carmel, though James does not name the place.

places.name: Land of Israel under Ahab
places.role: Elijah prayed that it would not rain, and the text says no rain fell for three and a half years. This detail is not in 1 Kings itself, which gives 'the third year' in 18:1.

setting.summary: The final chapter of the Letter of James warns rich landowners who withhold wages, urges believers to be patient until the 'coming of the Lord', and warns against swearing oaths. It ends with instructions on prayer for the sick, confession of sins, the example of Elijah, and bringing back someone who has wandered from the truth.
setting.title: Wealth, Patience, Prayer and Healing
setting.written: Traditionally written by James, the brother of Jesus and a leader of the Jerusalem church, probably before his death c. AD 62; many scholars instead date it later and think it may have been written in his name.

words.here: James uses prophetic language here. The rich are told to wail loudly, as people did when disaster was announced.
words.shift: The Greek verb sounds like the cry it describes. It is a rare word, used in the Greek Old Testament for prophets' cries of grief over coming judgment. Modern English "howl" suggests an animal, or an outburst of anger or laughter.
words.verse: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for your coming miseries.

words.here: The title is a rare one in the New Testament. It presents God as a commander who hears the cries of unpaid workers.
words.shift: Sabaōth is the Hebrew word tsĕvā'ôt written in Greek letters. It means armies or hosts. Many English Bibles translate it "Almighty", which loses the military picture. "Hosts" now sounds like party hosts or church liturgy.
words.verse: have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies.

words.here: James describes the rich as having lived in comfort at the expense of their workers. The word carries a note of excess.
words.shift: "Delicately" now suggests fine manners or fragile health. The Greek word means a soft, pampered life of excess. The English word hides the criticism of overindulgence.
words.verse: You have lived delicately on the earth, and taken your pleasure.

words.here: The readers are being wronged. The word asks them to hold back from retaliation while they wait, not just to wait quietly.
words.shift: Modern "patient" often means calmly waiting. The Greek is literally "long of spirit" or "long of temper", and it stresses self-restraint under pressure. It is the opposite of a short temper.
words.verse: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord.

words.here: James follows the example of Job with a description of God's character. The feeling is deep and personal, not distant.
words.literal: of many inner organs; very tender-hearted
words.shift: The Greek word comes from splanchna, the inner organs, which ancient people saw as the seat of deep feeling. English "pity" can sound condescending. The Greek suggests a gut-level compassion. The word is very rare and may have been coined in this form.
words.verse: the Lord is full of pity and merciful.

words.here: The verb sits next to "raise him up", so the sense may be physical recovery. Readers differ on how far it also means more than that.
words.shift: The verb is the usual New Testament word for "save". It can mean rescue from danger, physical healing or spiritual salvation. English "heal" narrows it to the body.
words.verse: The prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up.

words.here: James presents the prophet Elijah as an ordinary human being. That makes his prayer an example other people can look to.
words.shift: The word is the root of English "homeopathy" and "empathy", but it does not mean either. It means sharing the same condition as others, including suffering and limits. English "nature" sounds more abstract than the Greek.
words.verse: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain
